title: The end-to-end argument: idempotence from client to storage
goal: By the end, you can state the end-to-end argument, say where the connection's, the log's and the database's guards against repeats each stop, carry one id from a tap on the phone to a unique constraint at the final write, and size what keeping those ids costs.
opening:
You're on a train, sending 45.00 to a friend from your banking app. You tap send, the train enters a tunnel, and the spinner turns. Ten seconds later, the app sends the request again. Out of the tunnel, your balance is 90.00 lower.

Nothing broke. The bank's server saved the first transfer 80 ms after your tap; only its answer was lost in the tunnel. The app heard nothing and tried again, and the server saw a new, perfectly good transfer.

It's easy to think a stack of careful parts adds up to a careful whole. The connection numbers its bytes, the log drops resent messages, and the database saves each transaction once. Each promise is real, and none of them knows you meant one transfer.

Unbundling the database ended with a read that waits for its own write. That can't stop a retry from paying twice. In this lesson, we'll find where each layer's guard stops, and carry one id from your tap to the bank's records. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Your transfer travels over an encrypted connection to the bank's server, then through Kafka set to drop its own resent messages and count each record once, then into a PostgreSQL transaction at the strictest setting. The phone's request times out after the server has saved the transfer, and the phone sends it again. How many transfers does the bank record?
options: One, because every layer on the way promises exactly once
Two, because no layer on the way can tell the retry from a new transfer
One, because the connection's numbering of bytes drops the repeated request
None, because the timeout cancels the first transaction
warmup.why: Each promise holds inside its own layer and says nothing about the retry. The retry is a new connection with fresh byte numbers, a new message to Kafka with a new number, and a new, perfectly valid transaction. Only something that knows the two requests are one intent can drop the second, and that knowledge starts on the phone. The first option is the trap: piling up exactly-once layers feels as if it should add up to exactly once overall. The last option fails because the server's save doesn't know the phone stopped waiting.

sections.h: A retried transfer moves the money twice
sections.body:
Let's play the train ride in a small program and count. The phone sends a transfer of 45.00 from account acc-01 to acc-02. The server records it in the ledger, the bank's list of every movement of money, 80 ms later. The answer is lost. After its timeout, the phone sends the request again, on a new connection, and the server records that one too. In the Try it, two attempts make two ledger rows, and 90.00 leaves the account.

Which part was wrong? None of them, taken alone. TCP, the set of rules that carries bytes between the phone and the server, delivered each request exactly once on its connection. The database ran each transaction, a group of changes saved as one, and saved each one once. And the app did what a client, the program that sends requests, must do. When it hears nothing back, it can't tell whether the request was lost or only the answer (Partial failure, in the Faults, time and truth track). Retrying is the only way to make sure the transfer happens at all.

The duplicate exists only at a level none of those parts can see: you meant one transfer, and two arrived. The database can't know it. Two identical transfers a few seconds apart are as believable as a retry, because people do pay the same amount twice. Two-phase commit, from Atomic commit across machines, saves one change on several machines at once. It lets the program in charge find out whether a stuck transaction was saved, but the phone isn't part of it. The hop from the phone to the server is exactly where the doubt began. A common web trick, sending the browser to a fresh page after a form is sent (Post/Redirect/Get), doesn't help either. It only works once the answer has arrived.

So the knowledge that would let you drop the duplicate exists only on the phone, at the moment you tap send. The fix this lesson builds is to give that tap an identity, an id, and carry it to the place where money moves. The Try it plays the train ride twice. With a new id on every attempt, two attempts make two ledger rows. With one id per tap, and a rule at the ledger that each id may appear once, the same two attempts make one row.

Before we build it, let's see why every layer below the app has the same blind spot. A paper from 1984 explained it.

try.title: Lose one answer
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder. It sends one 45.00 transfer whose first answer is lost, so the phone retries once. It runs twice: with a new request id on every attempt, then with one id per tap and a check at the ledger that each id appears once.
Predict for each run: how many records reach the broker (the Kafka server that keeps the log), and how many rows reach the ledger?
In the second run, the broker still has two records. Why is that fine?

code.title: RetryDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
a new request id per attempt, no unique check:
  attempts sent: 2, ids req-000001, req-000002
  records in the broker: 2
  ledger row: req-000001 acc-01 -> acc-02 45.00
  ledger row: req-000002 acc-01 -> acc-02 45.00
  acc-01 1000.00 -> 910.00, moved 90.00
one request id per tap, UNIQUE (request_id) in the ledger:
  attempts sent: 2, ids req-000001, req-000001
  records in the broker: 2
  ledger row: req-000001 acc-01 -> acc-02 45.00
  acc-01 1000.00 -> 955.00, moved 45.00
```
Both runs put two records in the broker, because the server really did receive two requests. The second run is correct anyway. The duplicate is dropped at the last step, where the money moves, and nothing before that step had to be perfect.

sections.h: The end-to-end argument: only the two ends know what correct means
sections.body:
In 1984, Jerome Saltzer, David Reed and David Clark of MIT published "End-to-End Arguments in System Design". It asked where, in a system built in layers, a job belongs. Their worked case was copying a file from the disk of computer A to the disk of computer B without damage.

They listed what can go wrong. The disk at A can return bad data. The file system, the copying program or the network code can make a mistake while holding or copying the data, at either end. The processor or memory can make a one-off error during a copy. The network can drop, damage or duplicate packets, the small parcels data travels in. And either computer can crash partway through.

Now suppose the network promises reliable delivery, with checks, numbering and resending inside it. That fixes the network's faults and none of the others. A bug that damages the data in memory on computer B happens after the network has done its job perfectly.

The only complete check sits at the ends. Computer B reads the file back from its own disk and works out a checksum, a short number computed from every byte, so that any change to the bytes changes it. A compares it with the original's, and if they differ, they start again. That check is needed anyway, so a reliable network isn't needed for correctness. It only makes retries rarer, which is a speed gain. The paper's principle is that such a job can be done completely only by the application at the endpoints, the programs at each end. A partial version lower down is worth having only to make things faster.

The paper applies the same reasoning to **duplicate suppression**, spotting a repeat and not acting on it, and its example could be today's. A network that drops its own duplicate packets still can't drop the duplicates an app creates by retrying. When a user who gets no answer tries again, the network sees a new message.

The same argument covers two more jobs. One is integrity, keeping data undamaged. TCP's 16-bit checksum protects bytes while they cross one connection, and so does the tag that TLS, the encryption on web connections, adds to detect tampering. A bug in the server that damages an amount, or a bit that flips on a disk, happens outside any connection and passes every check. Trust, but verify, lesson 5 of this track, builds end-to-end checks for stored data. The other job is secrecy. TLS encrypts each hop, and a load balancer, a server that spreads requests over many servers, often ends the encrypted connection and reads the plain text. Encryption that must survive every machine in between needs keys that only the two ends hold.

None of this makes the lower layers useless. TCP's resending saves you from retrying a whole transfer after every lost packet.

**Lower layers make the common case fast. Correctness is checked at the ends.**

Next, let's put this to work on a transfer's real path, one layer at a time.

try.title: What each mechanism covers, and where it stops
steps: For each mechanism, write what it protects, and the first thing on the path from the phone to the ledger that it can't see.

1. TCP's numbering of bytes. 2. TLS between the phone and the load balancer. 3. Kafka's idempotent producer, which lets the broker drop a batch of records it was sent twice. 4. Kafka's exactly-once mode (transactions plus `read_committed`, which hides unfinished ones from readers). 5. A PostgreSQL transaction at SERIALIZABLE, its strictest isolation level. 6. Temporal, a program that reruns failed steps, retrying a step that asks the card's bank to take the money. 7. An `Idempotency-Key` sent to the card's bank. 8. A request id made on the phone and kept UNIQUE in the ledger.
try.expect:
1. Repeated and reordered bytes within one connection. Can't see: a retry on a new connection.
2. Eavesdropping and tampering between the phone and the load balancer. Can't see: anything after TLS ends, in plain text inside the bank's network.
3. A producer's own resend of a batch after a lost "got it". Can't see: a second send of the same transfer, which gets a new sequence number.
4. Reading, processing and writing within Kafka, with the saved offset in the same transaction. Can't see: a write to PostgreSQL, or a call to the card's bank, inside the loop.
5. Transactions running at once and interfering with each other. Can't see: two transactions that are both valid, one being a retry of the other.
6. A crashed or failed step being run again. Can't see: whether the bank already took the money the first time; it makes duplicates more likely, not less.
7. Duplicate charges at the card's bank, for retries that send the same key. Can't see: your own ledger.
8. The whole path: every retry of one tap, at any hop, is recognised at the final write. Its limit is time: a retry after the id is cleared out is new again (the last section).

refs.title: Saltzer, Reed and Clark, End-to-End Arguments in System Design (ACM TOCS, 1984)

sections.h: Every layer's exactly-once stops at its own edge
sections.body:
Here's the path a transfer takes in this lesson's lab, and the four faults the lab injects, one at each hop.

The phone sends the request over HTTP, the web's request-and-answer protocol, on TCP, to the API server, the bank's program that takes requests from apps. Fault one: the network delivers the request twice on that connection, a resend whose original wasn't lost after all. Fault two: the server saves the transfer, the answer is lost, and the phone retries on a new connection.

The server then writes a record to a Kafka topic, a log that the next program reads. A program that writes to Kafka is a producer, and the Kafka server that keeps the log is a broker. Fault three: the broker adds the record, its acknowledgement (its "got it") is lost, and the producer resends it. A consumer reads the record, inserts a ledger row in PostgreSQL, and then commits its offset, saving how far it has read. Fault four: the consumer dies after the insert and before saving its offset, so it's given the record again.

Each layer has its own guard, and each guard is right within its own range.

- TCP numbers every byte on a connection and drops bytes it has already delivered. It catches fault one. A retry opens a new connection with fresh numbers, so fault two gets through.
- Kafka's idempotent producer (Producers II: batching, acks and idempotence) tags each batch with a producer id and a sequence number, and the broker refuses a pair it has already added. Idempotent means safe to repeat. It catches fault three. But when the server handles the phone's retry, it sends the record again and gets the next sequence number, so fault two gets through again.
- Kafka's exactly-once mode, often called EOS (Transactions and exactly-once), saves a consumer's offset and the records it writes to Kafka together. The ledger row is in PostgreSQL, outside that transaction, so fault four leaves a row behind that Kafka can't take back.
- The database runs each transaction all or nothing. The retry from fault two and the redelivery from fault four are each a valid new transaction.

Durable execution engines have the same edge. Durable execution, in the Encoding track, showed that Temporal, a program that runs long tasks step by step and survives crashes, records each step's result once. The step itself may still run more than once.

The lab measures it. 1,000 transfers go through the same faults, with each guard switched on in turn. With none, the ledger ends up with 103 extra rows, and 53,025.23 moves that nobody asked to move. TCP's numbering brings it to 78, and the idempotent producer to 47. The 47 left are lost answers and consumer crashes, the two faults that happen above every layer: one in the phone's retry, one in the gap between two systems. A request id checked at the ledger brings it to 0.

The stepper follows one transfer through all four faults. Then we'll build that last guard.

```text
variant       duplicate rows      extra money
NONE                     103        53,025.23
TRANSPORT                 78        38,375.76

```
`TRANSPORT` is TCP's guard and `BROKER` the idempotent producer. Each lower layer removes its own share and no more, and no layer below the app gets to zero, because the remaining faults are retries and redeliveries that look new to everything below the ends. Another seed gives different counts with the same shape, and `END_TO_END` is 0 for every seed. The lab's property test checks that for 40 random seeds.

sections.h: One id, from the tap on the phone to a unique constraint
sections.body:
The fix has three parts, and each one is easy to get slightly wrong.

First, make the id where the intent is. The phone creates one id when you tap send, or when it shows the form, and keeps it for every attempt at that one transfer. A UUIDv7 works well. A UUID is a 128-bit id that nobody else will pick by chance, and version 7 starts with a timestamp. So new ids land at the right-hand edge of the database's B-tree index (the sorted structure behind most indexes), where the newest values go, instead of all over it. (PostgreSQL 18 makes one with `uuidv7()`.) The classic bug is making the id inside the retry loop. Every attempt then has its own id, and nothing further on can match them. The lab's phone ships with that bug.

Second, carry it through every hop. The id travels in the HTTP `Idempotency-Key` header, a labelled line at the top of a request. Calling other services, in the Encoding track, gave its rules, and Rate limiting and idempotency keys, in the Caching track, built a record in Redis, a fast in-memory store, that answers retries quickly. The IETF, the group that writes internet standards, has a draft for the header at revision 08 (October 2026); it isn't a finished standard yet. The API server copies the id into a header on the Kafka record, and the consumer copies it into the ledger row. Any hop that drops it, or makes a fresh one because that seemed tidier, reopens the hole for everything after it.

Third, enforce it at the final write, **in the same transaction as the effect**. The ledger table has the request id as its primary key, a column whose value no two rows may share. The consumer inserts the row with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, which skips the insert if the id is already there, and moves the money only if a row went in. In SQL, the language PostgreSQL speaks, the whole step is one statement:

```sql
WITH ins AS (
    INSERT INTO derive_ledger (request_id, from_account, to_account, cents)
    VALUES ('019a5e3c-4b7d-7f21-9c3e-2d4a6b8c0e1f', 'acc-01', 'acc-02', 4500)
    ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING
    RETURNING from_account, to_account, cents
)
UPDATE derive_accounts a
SET balance_cents = a.balance_cents
    + CASE WHEN a.account_id = ins.to_account THEN ins.cents ELSE -ins.cents END
FROM ins
WHERE a.account_id IN (ins.from_account, ins.to_account);
```

The first run reports `UPDATE 2`: two balances changed. Running the identical statement again, as a redelivery would, reports `UPDATE 0`, and the balances don't move. It holds even when two copies run at once, at PostgreSQL's default isolation level, read committed. (An isolation level says how strictly the database keeps transactions that run at the same time apart.) In the Try it, a second `psql` window runs the same statement while the first one's transaction is still open. It waits on the first one's entry in the unique index for 1.5 seconds, then reports `UPDATE 0`.

Why a constraint, and not a check in code? A `SELECT` for the id followed by an `INSERT` is check-then-act: look first, then act on what you saw. At read committed, two copies running at once both find nothing and both insert. That's the phantom problem from Write skew and phantoms, in the Transactions track: the row you check for doesn't exist yet, so there's nothing to lock. A 2015 study by Bailis and colleagues, "Feral Concurrency Control", found exactly this in apps built with Rails, a popular framework for web apps. Uniqueness checks in app code let duplicates through when requests arrived at the same time. The database checks a unique index at every isolation level.

**A check in code races. A unique constraint doesn't.**

The ledger table now also works as a log of every request that moved money, and balances could be derived from it, which is where Data integration started. Next, what keeping all those ids costs.

try.title: Post the same transfer twice, then twice at once
steps: From the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, then `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`. (Docker runs PostgreSQL in a container, a sealed-off box on your computer, and `psql` is its command-line client.)
Run the section's statement twice, then `SELECT * FROM derive_accounts ORDER BY 1;` and `SELECT count(*) FROM derive_ledger;`. Predict both before you look.

Now two at once. Open a second terminal with the same `psql` command. In the first: `BEGIN;`, then the statement with a new id (change `4b7d` to `aaaa`). Don't commit. In the second, run the same statement with the same new id. Watch it wait. Commit the first, and read the second's result.
Stop with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

code.title: what to check after the two runs

try.expect:
The two runs, then the checks:
```text
UPDATE 2
UPDATE 0
 account_id | balance_cents
------------+---------------
 acc-01     |         95500
 acc-02     |          4500
 ledger_rows
-------------
           1
 transaction_isolation
-----------------------
 read committed
```
The run with two sessions at once (here the first session kept its transaction open for 2 seconds):
```text
session A: BEGIN
session A: UPDATE 2
session B: (waits on A's uncommitted row in the unique index)
session A: COMMIT
session B: UPDATE 0        -- after waiting 1528 ms
```
The second insert can't tell whether its id is taken until the first transaction commits or rolls back, so it waits, then finds the row and does nothing. Had A rolled back, B's insert would have gone in. Either way, exactly one transfer happens, at read committed, without any lock in the app.

aside.title: Why can't the server make the id?
aside.body: Because the server can't tell a retry from a new request; that's the whole problem. A gateway that stamps a fresh id on each request it receives gives the retry a fresh id too. So does a web library that adds a new key to every attempt. The logs look tidy, since every request has a key, and two keys still arrive for one payment. Only the code that knows what you meant, before the first attempt, can make the id, and only a check inside the same transaction closes the gap.

sections.h: What the id costs: memory, space and care at every hop
sections.body:
The id isn't free, and each of its costs is a choice you make once.

The first is memory. The ledger has to **remember each id for as long as any client might still retry it**, because a retry after the id is forgotten is a new transfer. The Try it replays 100,000 transfers with realistic retry delays. Most retries come within seconds, some phones sat in the background for an hour, and a few were offline for days. A 1-minute window lets 292 duplicates through, 1 hour lets 184, 24 hours 9, and 7 days none. Stripe, a large payments company whose public API takes these keys, keeps them for at least 24 hours, and a key reused after it's cleared out starts a new request. For money, keep ids longer than the longest retry your clients can make. Or make clients stop retrying blindly past that age, and ask the server what happened instead.

That memory takes space. At 1,000 transfers a second, a 24-hour window holds 86.4 million ids: about 8.6 GB, at an assumed 100 bytes per id with its index entry. When the id is the ledger's own primary key, as in the SQL above, it's never forgotten, and the ledger carries that index forever. A separate request-id table, written in the same transaction and split into one piece, a partition, per day, lets old ids go with a cheap `DROP` of a whole partition. A `DELETE` would leave the table bloated with dead rows.

Every transfer also does one more write: a check and an insert in the unique index, in the same transaction. That's cheap with UUIDv7, whose inserts go to the right-hand edge of the index (B+trees, in the Storage engines track). With random UUIDv4 ids it's noticeably dearer, because each insert touches a random page, a block of the index on disk.

The id has to live where the effect lives, because the check must be in the same transaction. If the ledger is split across machines by account (the Partitioning track), key the id table by the paying account too, so the check and the money move on one machine.

A client that retries wants the result of its first attempt, and a bare "duplicate" error doesn't say whether the transfer went through. So the server keeps the first answer under the id and sends it again, the record that the Caching track's lesson built. It also stores a fingerprint of the request, a short hash of its contents, and rejects the same id with different contents (HTTP status 422 in the IETF draft). That's a client bug, not a retry.

Finally, the guarantee is only as good as the least careful program on the path. Code review has to treat "copies the request id into the outgoing record" like "checks the amount". When the server asks the card's bank to take the money, it sends an idempotency key made from the request id there too, so the bank also charges once.

A week of ids handles retries. It can't stop two different people from claiming the same thing at the same moment, and that's next.

try.title: How long must the ledger remember?
steps: Run the demo. It sends 100,000 transfers, 3% of them sent again later, after delays from a few seconds to three days, through a ledger that forgets ids older than its window.
Predict how many duplicates a 1-hour window lets through. More or less than 1 in 1,000?
Find the shortest window with no duplicates in this run, and read its storage cost. Is it worth it for transfers? For "like" buttons?

code.title: WindowDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
100,000 transfers, 2,891 sent again later
window       duplicate rows        id table at 1,000/s
1 minute                292           60,000 ids, 6 MB
1 hour                  184      3,600,000 ids, 360 MB
24 hours                  9     86,400,000 ids, 8.6 GB
7 days                    0   604,800,000 ids, 60.5 GB
```
An hour still lets 184 in 100,000 through, almost 2 per 1,000, because the phones that were offline retry after the window. Seven days removes them all in this run, at 60 GB of ids (the sizes assume 100 bytes per id). For transfers, that's cheap insurance. For a "like" button, a duplicate is harmless, and a minute is plenty. The window is a business decision with a number attached.

worked.title: Carry one id from the tap to the ledger

steps.say: **Make the id once, outside the retry loop.** The phone's intent is the tap, so the id belongs to the tap, not to an attempt.

**Know what each lower guard does, so you don't rely on it for more.** TCP drops a repeat inside one connection, and the idempotent broker drops a resend with the same producer id and sequence number. Both only make retries rarer here.
**Check the id and move the money in one step.** In the lab, that's one method; in PostgreSQL, one statement or one transaction.
**Choose the window from how long clients may retry.** A forgotten id makes a retry new again.

lab.title: Count duplicate ledger rows with each layer's guard, then fix it end to end
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 12 fail.

Read `Pipeline.kt` and `Faults.kt`; both are finished. `Server` opens a new `Connection` for every attempt and sends to the `Broker`. `Consumer` writes the `Ledger` and saves its offset, unless the fault plan crashes it in between. Each fault is decided by a hash of the event's name, so all four runs see the same faults.
In `Hops.kt`, write `Connection.receive` and `Broker.append`. The transport and broker tests in `HopsTest` pass.
Write `Ledger.postOnce`: refuse a request id that's already in `seen`; otherwise record it and post the row, in that one method.

Fix the bug in `Phone.send`: it makes a new id for every attempt. Run all the tests. `PipelineTest` checks the counts from this lesson (103, 78 and 47 duplicates for the first three guards, and 0 end to end), plus a property test over 40 random seeds.
hints: `Connection.receive`: keep `highestDelivered`; return null when `seq <= highestDelivered`, otherwise store `seq` and return the request.
`Broker.append`: when `idempotent`, `appended[producerId to seq]?.let { return it }` first. Then append a `Record(records.size.toLong(), request, trace)` and remember its offset under the pair.
`postOnce` must not call `post` when it returns false. If `the ledger posts a request id once` shows the money moved twice, check the order.
If `duplicates fall at each layer` shows END_TO_END above 0 while the ledger test passes, the phone is still sending a new id per attempt.

drill.title: The end-to-end write from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the PostgreSQL statement that records a transfer with request id `:rid` and moves the money only if the id is new. Then list, one line each, the guard at each of the four hops and the fault it can't see.

answer.src:
WITH ins AS (
    INSERT INTO ledger (request_id, from_account, to_account, cents)
    VALUES (:rid, :from, :to, :cents)
    ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING          -- a repeat inserts nothing
    RETURNING from_account, to_account, cents
)
UPDATE accounts a
SET balance_cents = a.balance_cents
    + CASE WHEN a.account_id = ins.to_account THEN ins.cents ELSE -ins.cents END
FROM ins                                         -- no row inserted: no money moves
WHERE a.account_id IN (ins.from_account, ins.to_account);

-- TCP sequence numbers: can't see a retry on a new connection
-- idempotent producer: can't see a second send() of the same transfer
-- Kafka exactly-once: can't see a write to the database inside the loop
-- the database transaction: can't tell a retry from a new transaction

recap: A client that hears nothing must retry, and it can't tell a lost request from a lost answer. So retries create duplicates that no lower layer can recognise.

The end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark, 1984): a job like spotting repeats, checking for damage or encrypting can be done completely only at the ends. Versions lower down only make it faster.

TCP drops repeats within one connection, the idempotent producer within one producer's resends, Kafka's exactly-once within Kafka, and a transaction within itself. In the lab they cut 103 duplicates to 78 and then 47, never to 0.

Make one id per intent on the client, carry it through every hop (HTTP header, Kafka record header) and enforce it with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the money movement. That gets to 0.
A unique index works at read committed. A check-then-insert in app code doesn't.

The limit: ids must be remembered for as long as any client may retry (24 hours of ids at 1,000 a second is about 86 million), each request costs an index write, the ids must live where the effect lives, and every hop must carry them.
closing:
We started on a train, with one tap that moved 90.00. Every layer kept its promise, and only the phone knew the two requests were one. One id made at the tap, carried through every hop and checked where the money moves, makes the second request harmless.

Next time a shop's app says "something went wrong" after you pay, check your bank's app before you tap again. If the payment shows up once, the shop most likely sends one id per tap.

Next, we'll stop two people claiming the same name at the same moment, without one lock over every machine, and find out which rules can be checked later and put right.

quiz.q: Your API returns each transfer's Kafka offset, and the app waits until the read model (the derived copy it reads balances from) has applied that offset before showing the new balance. Then the app's request times out after the server saved the transfer, and the app retries. Does the offset wait prevent a second transfer?
options: Yes: the app waits for the first transfer's offset, so it sees the first transfer and stops
No: the offset wait makes reads include your own write, but the retry is still a new write; only a request id checked at the ledger stops it
Yes, because the read model ignores records with an offset it has already applied
No, because offsets aren't returned for requests that time out
quiz.why: The offset wait from Unbundling the database makes a read include your own write. It does nothing about a retry, which the server treats as a new transfer with a new offset. The app never even got the first offset, because that answer is what was lost. The third option mixes up a consumer's own position with spotting repeats among different records.

quiz.q: A load balancer, the server that spreads requests over the payment servers, keeps long-lived TCP connections to each of them. It retries a request on another payment server after a 2-second timeout. Which mechanism can stop that retry from charging twice?
options: TCP's numbering of bytes, since the load balancer reuses its connections
TLS between the load balancer and the payment servers
A request id from the client, checked by a unique constraint where the charge is recorded
Setting the payment servers' database to SERIALIZABLE
quiz.why: The retry goes to another server over another connection, so TCP sees new bytes on a new connection; even on the same connection, a resent request is new bytes. TLS protects the bytes in transit and knows nothing about what they mean. Serializable isolation makes transactions that run at once behave as if one ran after the other, and a duplicate charge is a perfectly serializable history. Only an id that the client made, and that every attempt carries, identifies the retry.

quiz.q: A Kafka consumer reads `transfer-requested`, calls `producer.send()` to write a `ledger-entry` record, then crashes before saving its input offset. The producer has `enable.idempotence=true`. On restart, it handles the request again and sends again. What does the `ledger-entry` topic hold?
options: One record, because the idempotent producer drops the second send
Two records, because the second send is a new send with a new sequence number, maybe from a new producer id
One record, because the consumer's offset was never saved
Zero records, because the crash cancelled the first send
quiz.why: The idempotent producer drops its own resends of a batch after a lost "got it": same producer id, same sequence number. A send made after a restart is new work to the broker. Kafka's transactions can tie the output and the input offset together for exactly this loop, but only if you use them, and only for outputs that are Kafka records. The first option is the common belief that "idempotence" means the topic never holds duplicates.

quiz.q: Where should the request id for a transfer be made?
options: In the API gateway, the server that receives every request first, as each request arrives
In the consumer, from the Kafka record's offset
On the client, once per intent (when you tap send, or when the form is shown), and reused on every retry
In the database, from a counter, when the ledger row is inserted
quiz.why: Only the client knows that two requests are attempts at one intent, so the id must exist before the first attempt and be reused by every retry. A gateway sees each retry as a new request and gives it a new id. An offset identifies a record, and a retry produces a new record with a new offset. A database counter numbers rows, including duplicate ones.

quiz.q: The ledger keeps request ids for 1 hour. The mobile app saves transfers made offline and sends them when the phone reconnects, sometimes the next morning, with their original ids. What happens, and what's the fix?
options: Nothing goes wrong: the ids are unique, so the ledger accepts each one once

A transfer whose first attempt reached the server before the phone went offline is charged again; keep ids longer than the app may retry, or have the app ask for the transfer's status instead of resending old ones
The ledger rejects every transfer older than an hour
The app's retries fail with 409 Conflict until the id expires
quiz.why: After an hour, the ledger has forgotten the id, so a retry of a transfer that already happened looks new. The window has to cover the longest time a client may still retry. If there's no limit to that, the client must stop retrying blind and check the status first. The first option overlooks that uniqueness is only enforced for ids the ledger still remembers.

flashcards.front: The end-to-end argument in one sentence?
flashcards.back: Some jobs (spotting repeats, checking for damage, encrypting) can be done completely only by the programs at the two ends; versions lower down only make them faster.

flashcards.front: Why can't TCP drop a client's retry?
flashcards.back: The retry usually goes on a new connection with fresh numbers, and even on the same connection it's new bytes. TCP drops only resent bytes within one connection.

flashcards.front: What does Kafka's idempotent producer drop, and what not?
flashcards.back: A resend of the same batch by the same producer (same producer id and sequence number) after a lost "got it". Not a second send() of the same data.

flashcards.front: Where must the request id be enforced?
flashcards.back: At the final write, in the same transaction as the effect, with a unique constraint: for example INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING before moving the money.

flashcards.front: Why a unique constraint instead of SELECT, then INSERT?
flashcards.back: At read committed, two copies running at once both see no row and both insert. The database enforces a unique index at every isolation level.

flashcards.front: How long must request ids be kept?
flashcards.back: Longer than any client may still retry. A retry after the id is cleared out is a new request (Stripe clears keys after at least 24 hours).

terms.plain: Put a job where its correctness can be checked: at the two ends. Lower layers can only help it go faster.
An id for one intent, made by the client before the first attempt and sent with every retry. Also called an operation id or idempotency key.
Spotting a repeat of something already done, and not doing it again.
One whose effect is the same whether it runs once or many times.
Kafka's producer mode in which the broker drops a resent batch by its producer id and sequence number.
How long the system remembers ids. A retry after the window is treated as new.
A 128-bit id that starts with a millisecond timestamp, so ids are unique without asking anyone and roughly sorted by time.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "We use TLS, Kafka with exactly-once, and database transactions, so we can't charge anyone twice." Explain where that reasoning breaks, and what you'd add.
explain_back.answer: Each of those is correct inside its own layer, and blind to the duplicate that matters. When a phone's request times out after we saved the transfer, the phone retries. The retry is a new TLS session, a new TCP connection, a new Kafka send with a new sequence number and a new, valid database transaction. Kafka's exactly-once covers Kafka writes and offsets, so a consumer that dies after the database insert and before saving its offset writes the row again when it's given the record again. The only party that knows two requests are one payment is the client that sent them. So the client makes one id per payment before the first attempt and reuses it on every retry. Every hop copies it (HTTP header, Kafka record header, ledger column), and the ledger keeps it unique, checked in the same transaction that moves the money. The lower layers still matter, because they make retries rarer, but correctness comes from that one check. We also have to keep the ids at least as long as the app can retry, which for offline phones means days.

deeper.body:
**Saltzer, Reed and Clark's other examples.** The paper also applies the argument to delivery receipts (a network's "got it" says a message arrived, not that the program acted on it), to noticing that a computer crashed, and to keeping messages in order. Its warning is useful too: the argument isn't a rule that lower layers must be dumb. Where a lower layer can cheaply remove most failures, let it, and still check at the ends.

**Payments across machines without two-phase commit.** If the payer's and the payee's accounts live on different machines, the request id is what lets you skip two-phase commit. Add the request once to the payer's part of the log. A program that handles that part one request at a time checks the funds and writes a debit, a credit and a fee event, all carrying the request id, and every program further on applies events once per id. After a crash, the program reruns from its log, makes the same decision and writes the same ids, which the others ignore. Kleppmann, Beresford and Svingen describe this design in "Online Event Processing" (CACM, 2019), and lesson 4 of this track builds the rule-checking side of it.

**Stripe's v2 API goes further.** For API v1, Stripe stores the first answer under the key and sends it again, errors included. For API v2, a retry with the same key finishes work that failed or stopped halfway, when it can, instead of repeating an old failure. That's the same end-to-end idea, with the server taking on more of the recovery.

**Exactly-once is a property of effects.** Every system that advertises exactly-once (Kafka, Flink, Temporal, AWS Step Functions) delivers or runs things at least once, and arranges for the effect to count once, within its own edge. When you cross that edge, you bring your own id.

The framing of exactly-once effects, the end-to-end argument applied to data systems and the request-id pattern follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13.
